fixes.explanation: Torn off is right. Daniel says, “I watched until its wings were torn off…” The beast starts out looking ready to fly and ends up on its feet. After that it's lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man.
Lying down isn't what the text says. The beast is already raised up on one of its sides. Then it's told, “Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!” The words it hears are about getting up.
The sea isn't part of this one. Daniel says the fourth beast “…devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left.” The text gives trampling, and it says nothing about dragging.
That's right. Three of the first horns “…were uprooted before it.” Daniel says. The little horn comes up and three of the ten are gone. For a little horn, that's a big effect.
Not prayer, friend. The little horn has a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. That's what holds Daniel's attention. So that mouth isn't praying.

Seventy elders are on Mount Sinai in another story. Moses, Israel's leader, went up, and seventy elders of Israel went with him (Exodus 24:9). Daniel's vision has a far bigger crowd. Thousands upon thousands attend the Ancient of Days.

No bowing is mentioned, friend. Daniel says, “…the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.” That's the end of that beast. The verse says nothing about it kneeling.
Serve is right. He's given dominion, glory and kingship. Daniel says it's “…that the people of every nation and language should serve Him.” That's every nation and every language.

That's right. Daniel says, “…His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” His dominion is everlasting and will not pass away. Compare that with the rest of the beasts, whose dominion was removed (Daniel 7:12).

The text doesn't mention any sharing, friend. It says the dominion of the rest of the beasts was removed (Daniel 7:12). Daniel says of this One, “…His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” It's His, and it lasts.

Daniel did pray toward Jerusalem, three times a day with his windows open (Daniel 6:10). That's not what this verse says. Here he approaches one of those standing there and asks the true meaning of all this. The question comes first.
Forever and ever, baker. The explainer says the saints “…will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.” He says it twice. That's the kind of repeating I can get behind.
The other beasts aren't named there, baker. Daniel says, “…this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them…” It's a heavy moment. The war is aimed at the saints.

Gabriel does show up in Daniel's book. In Daniel 8:16 a voice calls for Gabriel to help Daniel understand a vision. In this verse, though, it's the Ancient of Days who arrives. He's the one who pronounces judgment in favor of the saints.

That's right. The explainer says the saints “…will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” It's a heavy stretch, and the text gives it in exactly those words. I won't try to turn it into a number.

Forty days and forty nights is how long the rain fell in the flood of Noah, who built the ark (Genesis 6:14; 7:12). That's a different story. Here the explainer says the saints will be given into his hand “…for a time, and times, and half a time.” The words here are different.
